title-group.article-title: Efficacy and Safety of Evolocumab in Improving Low-Density Lipoprotein Cholesterol (LDL-C) Levels in a Japanese Population ― Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis ―

sec.title: Background
sec.p: Hypercholesterolemia is a major risk factor for cardiovascular disorders. Evolocumab is efficacious and safe for the management of low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C); however, evidence supporting the utility of evolocumab in Japanese patients is lacking. To fill this evidence gap, we conducted this systematic review and meta-analysis.

sec.title: Methods and Results
sec.p: PubMed, EMBASE, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library from inception to October 2023 were searched for relevant publications. The primary outcomes were LDL-C levels and coronary artery plaque regression or stabilization. The secondary outcome was the incidence of adverse events. Nine studies were included: 6 randomized control trials (RCTs) and 3 cohort studies. The meta-analysis showed that evolocumab significantly reduced LDL-C levels in RCTs in the short (≤1 month), medium (≤3 months), and long (1 year) term, with a mean difference (MD) relative to placebo/standard of care (SOC) of −52.06% (95% confidence interval [CI] −59.32%, −44.79%), −69.12% (95% CI −71.45%, −66.79%), and −78.08% (95% CI −82.98%, −73.18%), respectively, and in the mid- to long (≤6 months) term in a cohort study, with an MD of −57.81% (95% CI −74.37%, −41.25%). Evolocumab also increased fibrous cap thickness and reduced macrophage grade. Adverse events were rare across included studies.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: Evolocumab seems to be effective and safe in reducing the LDL-C levels and leading to plaque regression/stabilization in Japanese patients.
Key Words: Efficacy, Evolocumab, Japanese patients, Meta-analysis, Safety
Received 2025 Jun 3; Revised 2025 Jun 10; Accepted 2025 Jun 12; Collection date 2025 Oct 10.

body.p: Hypercholesterolemia is a major established risk factor for cardiovascular disorders, especially coronary artery disease.1–3 Cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) are widely prevalent globally.4 Although there are trends for decreasing low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) concentrations in some countries,5,6 high LDL-C concentrations were still associated with approximately 4.4 million deaths in 2019.7 In Japan, CVDs are major contributors to death and requirements for long-term care.8 Over the period 2012–2022, the number of hospitalizations for acute myocardial infarction (AMI) increased in Japan, from 69,219 in 2012 to 80,084 in 2022.9 Previous studies have shown that LDL-C-lowering therapy leads to significant reductions in both major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) and mortality.10,11 However, even with most clinical guidelines recommending intensive LDL-C-lowering therapy for primary and secondary prevention of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD),12–14 LDL-C control remains challenging.6,15,16 In a recent study using medical claims database, LDL-C goals were achieved by 65.5%, 60.6%, and only 25.4% of patients overall among those receiving LDL-C-lowering therapy for primary prevention, secondary prevention, and secondary prevention with a high risk of ASCVD, respectively.17 Among patients treated with intensive statin monotherapy for primary prevention, secondary prevention, and secondary prevention with a high risk of ASCVD, the rates of achieving LDL-C goals were 83.9%, 75.3%, and 29.5%, respectively.17

Proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (PCSK9) is associated with low-density lipoprotein receptor (LDLR) degradation, and gain-of-function mutations in PCSK9 trigger LDLR depletion and hyperlipidemia.18 To achieve better LDL-C control, some new drugs have been introduced into clinical practice, including ezetimibe and the PCSK9 inhibitor evolocumab. Besides statins, ezetimibe is the most used LDL-C-lowering drug. Ezetimibe can be used as monotherapy or in combination with a statin.19 However, in Japanese patients with a high risk of ASCVD, LDL-C goals were only achieved by 46.6% of those treated with a combination of ezetimibe and a statin.17

Thus, there is a need for a strong cholesterol-lowering drug in clinical practice. As a PCSK9 inhibitor, evolocumab has shown significant efficacy and safety in the management of LDL-C in previous studies.20–26 Since its approval for use in Japan in 2016, evolocumab has been used widely and consistently.27 However, evidence supporting the efficacy and safety of evolocumab in Japanese patients is lacking. To address this question, we conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized clinical trials (RCTs) and real-world studies.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: This systematic review and meta-analysis was performed in accordance with the PRISMA extension statement. This study protocol has been registered with PROSPERO (Registration no. CRD420250651163).

sec.title: Data Sources and Search Strategy
sec.p: PubMed, EMBASE, Web of Science, the Cochrane Library, from inception to October 17, 2023, were searched for relevant publications by experienced information specialists using the keywords, “evolocumab”, “anti-PCSK-9”, and “Japan”, without limitation on language. There were no limitations on date, document type, or publication status. Detailed search strategies used in each of the databases are presented in the Supplementary Appendix.

sec.title: Study Selection
sec.p: The inclusion and exclusion criteria used for determination of first-level study eligibility and the exclusion criteria for second-level screening are presented in Table 1. Duplicates found and confirmed during the literature screening process were excluded. For multiple reports of the same study, only the most recent publication was included and the rest were used as references. Based on the inclusion and exclusion criteria, 2 reviewers independently screened the titles and abstracts using Rayyan online software (https://www.rayyan.ai/) for the first-level screening. Then, each of the articles identified in the first-level screening underwent full-text screening by 2 reviewers independently. Any disagreement was resolved through discussion between the 2 reviewers and, if necessary, a third reviewer. The study selection process (PRISMA flow diagram) is shown in Supplementary Figure 1.

sec.title: Data Extraction
sec.p: Data from each study were extracted independently by 2 reviewers using a standardized data extraction form. Any disagreement was resolved by discussion or with the assistance from a third reviewer if consensus could not be reached. The information extracted included: general study characteristics (first author, publication year, sample size, study design, study/data period); baseline patient characteristics (sex, age, LDL-C level); intervention measures (evolocumab treatment [monotherapy or combined with other drugs], treatment in the control group, and duration of treatment); and primary (LDL-C level, coronary artery plaque regression or stabilization) and secondary (incidence of relevant adverse events) outcomes.

sec.title: Quality Assessment
sec.p: Two reviewers independently assessed the risk of bias of the included studies, with any inconsistencies resolved by a third reviewer. The risk of bias of RCTs was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool (RoB 1.0), with domains including randomization, allocation concealment, blinding of participants and personnel, blinding of outcome assessment, incomplete outcome data, selective outcome reporting, and other bias. For non-randomized studies of intervention and cohort studies, the Newcastle Ottawa Scale (NOS) was used to evaluate internal authenticity.

sec.title: Data Synthesis and Statistical Analysis
sec.p: Under the premise of acceptable clinical and methodological heterogeneity, a meta-analysis was conducted for the primary outcome. A fixed-effect model was used for meta-analyses via RevMan 5.3 or R version 4.2.2 software, in which a single group rate meta-analysis was conducted using the model from meta-package 6.1.0.28 Before performing the meta-analysis, the homogeneity of studies was checked in terms of the characteristics of the study population, the intervention used, outcomes, study design, and statistical metrics. If a meta-analysis was feasible, the outcomes were summarized using mean differences (MDs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for continuous variables and risk ratios (RRs) with 95% CIs for dichotomous variables. RCTs and non-randomized controlled study designs were analyzed separately. If a meta-analysis was considered inappropriate, the outcome data were summarized narratively. Statistical heterogeneity was estimated via I2 and χ2 statistics (substantial statistical heterogeneity was defined as I2 ≥50% with a P<0.1 in a χ2 test).

sec.title: Characteristics of Included Studies and Participants
sec.p: The initial search retrieved a total of 398 articles. After the removal of duplicates, 242 unique articles remained. In accordance with the inclusion and exclusion criteria in the first-level screening, 183 articles were excluded based on title and abstract screening. During full-text screening, 13 articles were excluded because they focused on populations other than the Japanese, another 13 articles were excluded because they did not align with the comparisons of interest, 9 articles were excluded because they were neither a real-world study nor an RCT, 3 articles were excluded because the full text was not available, 4 articles were excluded because they lacked focused outcome data, and 5 articles were excluded because they were different publications of the same study without additional information or duplicated literature. Ultimately, 12 articles from 9 studies were included29–37 (Supplementary Figure 1).

Nine studies with 1,691 participants were included in this review (Table 2); 6 were RCTs29,30,33–36 and 3 were cohort studies.31,32,37 All studies were focused on the Japanese population with statins as background therapy. The mean age of patients in the included studies ranged from 61 to 74.2 years. Two studies reported outcomes after 1 month of treatment, 4 studies reported outcomes at 3 months, 1 study reported outcomes at 6 months, and another study reported outcomes at 1 year.

sec.title: Quality Assessment
sec.p: The internal validity of the 6 included RCTs was assessed using RoB 1.0. Considering that 4 studies did not report the specific method of random sequence generation, 5 studies did not report the method of allocation concealment, 4 studies did not report the implementation of blinding in detail, and 1 study lacked a conflict of interest statement, we rated the risk of bias of the corresponding domains as unclear risk (Supplementary Figure 2). The NOS was used to evaluate risk of bias of cohort studies, with no obvious risk of bias being found (Supplementary Table 1).

sec.title: Efficacy of Evolocumab
sec.p: Evidence from RCTs showed that, compared with the control group, evolocumab treatment effectively reduced LDL-C levels by 66.90% at 1 month, 69.23% at 3 months, and 70.71% at 1 year (Table 3). In cohort studies, compared with the control group, evolocumab treatment effectively reduced LDL-C levels by 57.51% at 3 months and by 71.87% at 6 months (Table 3). Forest plots of data from the included studies are shown in Figures 1,2 and Supplementary Figures 3,4. Evolocumab treatment also yielded benefits in terms of plaque regression/stability (Table 4).

sec.p: Short-Term (≤1 Month) Efficacy The meta-analysis results of 2 RCTs34,36 showed that, compared with placebo or standard of care, evolocumab significantly reduced LDL-C levels by 52.06% (MD −52.06; 95% CI −59.32, −44.79; I2=87%; P<0.00001) in the short (≤1 month) term (Figure 1A). From these RCTs, the difference in the short-term (≤1 month) reduction in LDL-C between the evolocumab and control groups was 53.39 mg/dL (MD −53.39; 95% CI −58.58, −48.20; I2=0%, P<0.00001; Figure 1B).34,36 The pooled result of the short-term (≤1 month) reduction in LDL-C in the control group was 79.80 mg/dL (95% CI 75.40, 84.20; Supplementary Figure 3); thus, the MD/control ratio is −66.90±45.62%.

Medium-Term (≤3 Months) Efficacy The meta-analysis results of 3 RCTs29,30,33 showed that, compared with placebo or standard of care, evolocumab significantly reduced LDL-C levels by 69.12% (MD −69.12; 95% CI −71.45, −66.79; I2=93%; P<0.00001) in the medium (≤3 months) term (Figure 2A). In addition, a cohort study31 showed that, compared with placebo or standard of care, evolocumab significantly reduced LDL-C levels by 35.82% (MD −35.82; 95% CI −44.16, −27.48) in the medium (≤3 months) term (Table 3). Meta-analysis results of the 3 RCTs29,30,33 showed that the difference in medium-term (≤3 months) reductions in LDL-C between the evolocumab and control groups was 79.25 mg/dL (MD −79.25; 95% CI −81.98, −76.53; I2=96%; P<0.00001; Figure 2B). The pooled result of medium-term (≤3 months) reductions in LDL-C in the control group was 114.48 mg/dL (95% CI 112.15, 116.81; Supplementary Figure 4), thus the MD/control ratio is −69.23±43.23% (Table 3). In the cohort study,31 the difference in medium-term (≤3 months) reductions in LDL-C between the evolocumab and control groups was 42.10 mg/dL (MD −42.10; 95% CI −48.66, −35.54), thus the MD/control ratio is −57.51±34.10% (Table 3).

Mid- and Long-Term (≤6 Months) Efficacy In a cohort study,32 evolocumab, compared with placebo or standard of care, significantly reduced LDL-C levels by 57.81% (MD −57.81; 95% CI −74.37, −41.25) in the mid- to long term (≤6 months; Table 3). In the same study,32 the difference in mid- to long-term (≤6 months) reductions in LDL-C between the evolocumab and control groups was 49.30 mg/dL (MD −49.30; 95% CI −59.93, −38.67), thus the MD/control ratio is −71.87±77.28% (Table 3).

Long-Term (1 Year) Efficacy An RCT33 showed that, compared with placebo or standard of care, evolocumab significantly reduced the LDL-C levels by 78.08% (MD −78.08 95% CI −82.98, −73.18) in the long (1 year) term (Table 3). In the same RCT,33 with statins used as background therapy, the difference in long-term (1 year) reductions in LDL-C between the evolocumab and control groups was 92.41 mg/dL (MD −92.41; 95% CI −97.55, −87.27), thus the MD/control ratio is −70.71±47.31% (Table 3).

Plaque Regression/Stability Two studies31,32 reported that evolocumab could stabilize vulnerable coronary plaques and reduce plaque size. In addition, adding evolocumab, compared with statin monotherapy, increased fibrous cap thickness and reduced macrophage grade, as assessed by optical coherence tomography. These desirable outcomes provided a benefit in preventing the progression of coronary artery disease. However, the specific outcomes reported in these 2 studies are quite different; therefore, a meta-analysis was not feasible and the results are summarized in Table 4.

sec.title: Safety
sec.p: The incidence of related adverse events was very low in both the intervention (evolocumab) and control groups, so no definite conclusions could be drawn (Supplementary Tables 2–6).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: This systematic review and meta-analysis summarized the efficacy and safety of evolocumab for Japanese patients when using statins as background therapy. The results show that short-, medium-, and long-term treatment with evolocumab resulted in significant reductions in LDL-C levels, with acceptable safety, despite background statin therapy. Evolocumab was also beneficial for the stabilization of coronary plaque.

In this study we evaluated the efficacy of evolocumab according to treatment duration. Our results show that for Japanese patients receiving background statin therapy, short-term (≤1 month) evolocumab treatment reduced LDL-C levels by more than 50%, which suggests that evolocumab has a quick and significant effect on LDL-C levels. In fact, it was recently demonstrated that evolocumab has a very rapid (within 4 h) and effective suppressive impact on circulating unbound PCSK9, which resulted in a significant reduction in LDL-C concentrations 48 h after injection, with a full effect after 7–10 days.38 This effect may have important clinical value. As demonstrated in previous studies,19,39,40 patients with acute coronary syndrome (ACS) often have high LDL-C levels at the onset of ACS, and quick and efficacious reductions in LDL-C concentrations help maintain the efficacy of percutaneous coronary intervention for culprit and non-culprit lesions and reduce MACE during follow-up. In one study, after administration of a single dose of evolocumab to hospitalized ACS patients, LDL-C concentrations decreased from 109.0 to 41.4 mg/dL as early as 72 h after injection.41 In a prospective randomized controlled study, LDL-C concentrations in patients treated with evolocumab (140 mg every 2 weeks combined with atorvastatin 40 mg/day and ezetimibe 10 mg/day) decreased significantly and remained stable after 1 month.42 Follow-up at 3 months showed that the evolocumab had better efficacy and similar safety.42 These results suggest that evolocumab can lower LDL-C concentrations in a short time, which is supported by the results of our meta-analysis.

Evolocumab also showed good performance in reducing LDL-C (by 69.12%) over a ≤3-month treatment period in Japanese patients. Compared with short-term treatment (52.06% reduction in LDL-C), there appeared to be a trend for further reduction in LDL-C levels with longer-term evolocumab treatment. In a retrospective study, 6-month evolocumab treatment resulted in a 57.81% reduction in LDL-C concentrations.32 In the open-label extension of YUKAWA studies, Hirayama et al. investigated the efficacy and safety of 1-year treatment with evolocumab in a pooled analysis of Japanese patients.33 In that study, the rate of LDL-C reduction was 65.1–69.1% among Japanese patients receiving evolocumab plus standard of care.33 Taking these results into consideration, we believe that the effects of evolocumab are stable and significant. In a recent observational cohort study, LDL-C was reduced by >50% within 3 months and efficacy was maintained over 12 months after evolocumab treatment.43 In another cohort study from Spain, evolocumab showed a significant and sustained reduction in LDL-C levels during 30 months of follow-up.44 In the final results from the European observational HEYMANS study, evolocumab therapy was also associated with sustained reductions in LDL-C up to 30 months.45 In that study, of patients in whom LDL-C levels were monitored, approximately 85% achieved a ≥30% reduction from baseline at each follow-up visit and 60% achieved a ≥50% reduction.45 After the milestone Scandinavian Simvastatin Survival Study (4S) demonstrated for the first time that long-term cholesterol-lowering treatment with statin was safe and improved survival in patients with coronary heart disease,46 more and more evidence has accumulated that continuous and aggressive LDL-C reduction is critical for patients with ASCVD,47–49 and this could be correlated with continuous inhibition of plaque progression and even regression.50 Based on these findings, it is reasonable to believe that long-term treatment with evolocumab will be beneficial for patients with hypercholesterolemia.

Evolocumab also had favorable effects in stabilizing vulnerable coronary plaques, reducing plaque volume and macrophage infiltration, and ameliorating fibrous cap thickness. In addition to the many imaging studies that show plaque stabilization with LDL-C-lowering drugs, several recent reports have illustrated the effectiveness of early statin and PCSK9 inhibitor therapy in rapidly stabilizing non-culprit coronary plaques.51 These effects are important in decreasing the risk of MACE in patients with established ASCVD or hypercholesteremia.52,53 The FOURIER trial evaluated the clinical efficacy and safety of evolocumab in 27,564 patients with ASCVD. Evolocumab in combination with statin led to a significant reduction in MACE after 2.2 years follow-up. Further, the FOURIER-OLE trial reaffirmed the results observed in the original FOURIER trial during an extended median follow-up period of 4.8 years.25 In a recent meta-analysis, evolocumab was associated with a reduction in the risks of myocardial infarction, ischemic stroke, and coronary revascularization.54 In another recent meta-analysis that included 11 RCTs involving 24,732 patients with ACS or who experienced recent episodes, the incidence of myocardial infarction and cerebrovascular events was significantly lower in the group treated with a PCSK9 inhibitor than in the placebo group.55

The 2023 Japanese Circulation Society guideline suggests that for patients with elevated LDL-C concentrations, achieving target goals based on comprehensive risk assessment should be prioritized through lifestyle interventions and cholesterol-lowering treatments such as statins.56 Due to significant protective effects of statins on patients with ASCVD, most studies of evolocumab were designed to use evolocumab in combination with statins, or in patients who were statin intolerant or had familial hypercholesterolemia. That is, the comparison was often made between statin and evolocumab plus statin,29–32,57 or between evolocumab and placebo/ezetimibe.58 Most results supported the superiority of evolocumab plus statin over statin alone or that of evolocumab over placebo or ezetimibe. A previous animal study compared evolocumab with evolocumab plus statin in male rabbits and found that, compared with evolocumab monotherapy, the combination of evolocumab and atorvastatin resulted in a greater reduction in serum concentrations of total cholesterol, triglyceride, and low-density lipoprotein.59 Further, the same team found that the combination of evolocumab and atorvastatin in rabbit model resulted in a more statistically significant reduction in Toll-like receptor expression and intimal thickness,60 which suggests that the combination of evolocumab and atorvastatin may be more beneficial than evolocumab alone in ASCVD. Further clinical studies comparing evolocumab monotherapy with statin in terms of reductions in LDL-C and/or improvements in prognosis in patients with ASCVD or hypercholesterolemia are warranted.

In the present study, we found no significant increase in the risk of adverse events in Japanese patients treated with evolocumab. None of the included studies reported hemorrhagic stroke or cognitive disorders, and the incidence of allergy, liver disorders, and muscle-related adverse events was very low. These findings are consistent with some previous studies. In terms of safety, existing studies have demonstrated that evolocumab has a very low risk of adverse events, especially severe adverse events. A large meta-analysis including 39 RCTs and 66,478 patients concluded that PCSK9 inhibitors was not associated with an increased risk of neurocognitive adverse events, increases in liver enzymes, rhabdomyolysis, or new-onset diabetes.61 A recent systematic review and meta-analysis addressed the efficacy and safety of evolocumab compared with other lipid-lowering therapies or placebo and found no statistically significant relationship for the risk of adverse effects, serious adverse effects, and MACE with evolocumab treatment compared with placebo (relative risk 1.04; 95% CI 0.99, 1.08; P=0.12).54

sec.title: Study Strengths and Limitations
sec.p: This study has some strengths. First, this is the first systematic review and meta-analysis evaluating the efficacy and safety of evolocumab specifically in Japanese patients. Previous studies have demonstrated the impact of race on cholesterol levels and the efficacy of lipid-lowering drugs,62,63 and the evidence specifically for Japanese patients needs to be summarized. Second, this study summarizes the short-, medium-, and long-term efficacy of evolocumab, providing information regarding the continuous LDL-C-lowering performance of evolocumab. Third, this study was conducted in strict accordance with the PRISMA extension statement, which make the results objective and reliable. With the findings of the present study, we believe it is reasonable to treat Japanese patients with evolocumab.

This study also has some limitations. First, the significant heterogeneity of the included studies made it difficult to perform some analyses, especially safety evaluation. We have used tables to show the safety of evolocumab; as indicated in Table 2, the diseases of the populations in the included studies were inconsistent. Second, for some analysis, only 1–2 studies were available. More evidence in the Japanese population is needed. We also included some cohort studies, which results in a relatively lower degree of certainty regarding conclusions drawn from the evidence. Third, this study had no evidence regarding the efficacy and safety of evolocumab for treatment duration >12 months. A clinical study with a longer duration (>12 months) of evolocumab treatment in Japanese patients is warranted in the future.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: Evolocumab therapy seems to be effective and safe in reducing the LDL-C concentrations in the Japanese population. The evidence suggests that evolocumab therapy is also effective in regressing/stabilizing plaque and reducing the incidence of adverse events.
